issues.legal_issue: A jurist’s public opposition to a person’s elevation, based on allegations against that person, may create a reasonable apprehension of bias when the jurist is later appointed to investigate those allegations.
material_facts: The jurist publicly opposed the subject’s elevation and advocated a public inquiry into allegations against him.
The jurist drafted a resolution opposing the elevation and participated in a campaign concerning the allegations.
The jurist had no personal dispute with the subject, and the subject had earlier met him and believed he had nothing against him.
issues.conclusion: The subject’s apprehension of a likelihood of bias was reasonable, although the Court did not find that the jurist was actually biased. The Court requested that another distinguished jurist be nominated in his place; because the charges had already been framed, the reconstituted committee could proceed on those charges.
issues.legal_principle: The rule against bias is part of natural justice and requires both impartial decision-making and the appearance of impartiality. For non-pecuniary bias, the applicable test is whether a fair-minded, informed and reasonable person, considering all the relevant facts, would apprehend a real likelihood or possibility of bias; proof of actual bias is unnecessary. The Court applied the principles in Manak Lal v. Dr. Prem Chand Singhvi, A.K. Kraipak v. Union of India, S. Parthasarthi v. State of A.P., Dr. G. Sarana v. University of Lucknow, Ranjit Thakur v. Union of India, Secretary to Government, Transport Department v. Munuswamy Mudaliar, and Bihar State Mineral Development Corporation v. Encon Builders (I) (P) Ltd. The inquiry committee was constituted under Section 3(2)(c) of the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968, within the constitutional framework of Articles 121, 124(4) and 124(5), read with Article 217; the investigation also carries the fair-hearing requirements in Sections 3 and 4 of the Act.

predicates.judicial_misconduct_inquiry: A committee was appointed to investigate alleged misbehaviour or incapacity by a judicial office-holder.
predicates.member_publicly_opposed_subject_elevatio: A committee member publicly opposed the subject’s elevation and advocated inquiry into allegations against the subject.

issues.definition: When a committee member publicly opposes the subject’s elevation based on allegations against the subject in a judicial-misconduct inquiry, the rule treats a reasonable apprehension of bias as established.

issues.legal_issue: A person who knows the facts supporting an objection to an inquiry committee member and knowingly delays raising that personal objection may waive the right to rely on it to invalidate proceedings.
material_facts: The subject knew that the jurist was a committee member by May 2010 and knew of the jurist’s public opposition to his elevation.
The subject did not object to the jurist’s membership in earlier communications, including a request that the inquiry be expedited.
The subject first objected after receiving the notice of charges and the lists of supporting documents and witnesses.
The objection concerned a right personal to the subject, and the inquiry had proceeded only to the framing of charges.
issues.conclusion: The subject waived the right to object to the jurist’s appointment and could not obtain invalidation of the committee’s proceedings on that basis. The writ petition was dismissed, while the Court requested the Chairman to nominate another jurist and permitted the reconstituted committee to proceed on the charges already framed.
issues.legal_principle: A person may waive a right conferred for that person’s individual protection if the person knows the relevant facts and the right, and no public right or public policy is infringed. Failure to object alone does not invariably establish waiver, but waiver may be inferred where a person knowingly remains silent and raises the objection only after proceedings have advanced. The Court relied on Manak Lal v. Dr. Prem Chand Singhvi, Lachhu Mal v. Radhey Shyam, and Dhirendra Nath Gorai v. Sudhir Chandra. The timing of the objection was also considered in the context of the investigation under the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968 and the time for submission of the committee’s report under Rule 9(2)(c) of the Judges (Inquiry) Rules, 1969.

rule.if: judicial_misconduct_inquiry and objector_knew_member_appointment and objector_knew_basis_for_bias_objection and objector_knew_right_to_object and objection_raised_only_after_charges_notice and objection_is_personal

predicates.judicial_misconduct_inquiry: A committee was appointed to investigate alleged misbehaviour or incapacity by a judicial office-holder.
predicates.objector_knew_member_appointment: The person under inquiry knew that the challenged person was a member of the committee.
predicates.objector_knew_basis_for_bias_objection: The person under inquiry knew the facts said to give rise to bias before raising the objection.
predicates.objector_knew_right_to_object: The person under inquiry knew that the committee member’s appointment could be challenged.
predicates.objection_raised_only_after_charges_noti: The person under inquiry first objected after receiving notice of the charges and the supporting materials.
predicates.objection_is_personal: The objection concerns a right for the individual protection of the person under inquiry, rather than a public right.

issues.definition: When a person in a judicial-misconduct inquiry knows the committee appointment, the basis and the right to object, but raises a personal objection only after receiving the charges notice, the objection is treated as waived and cannot invalidate the earlier proceedings.
